How a Concrete Driveway Is Installed, Step by Step

A concrete driveway installation in Florida runs about a week from tear-out to the point it can take light traffic: a day for demolition and excavation, a day for base and forms, a pour day timed around the heat, and a minimum 3-day cure. As of October 2026, full design strength isn't reached until about 28 days after the pour.

By the Opera Concrete & Pavers estimating team · Updated October 1, 2026

What's the Realistic Timeline From Tear-Out to a Drivable Driveway?

A standard residential concrete driveway runs about a week from the first day of demolition to the point it can carry a car, though a straightforward new pour on bare ground with no old slab to remove can move faster, and a large or oddly shaped driveway runs longer. Most of that week isn't the pour itself, which usually takes a few hours once the truck arrives; it's excavation, base compaction and the curing days afterward that set the actual schedule.

A typical concrete driveway installation, day by day
DayWhat happens
1Old driveway demolished and hauled off, if one exists; new site excavated to depth
2Subgrade compacted, forms set, base material placed and compacted
3Concrete delivered and poured, screeded, floated and finished; control joints cut the same day
4–6Curing under plastic sheeting, a curing compound or wet curing; no traffic on the slab
7Light vehicle traffic typically allowed; full design strength isn't reached until 28 days

Sequence and timing from NRMCA's own guidance on joints, hot-weather placing and curing (NRMCA CIP 6, NRMCA CIP 12).

What Happens on Demolition and Excavation Day?

Where an old driveway is coming out, it's broken up and hauled off before anything new goes in, and the exposed ground is then excavated to the combined depth the base and the new slab need together. On a typical Florida lot, that means digging past the topsoil's organic layer to firmer sand, since anything with roots, mulch or loose fill left under a slab compacts unevenly later and shows up as a settled spot within a season or two. Old concrete that's reinforced with rebar or wire mesh takes longer to break out than plain slabs, since the steel has to be cut free rather than just cracked and lifted.

What Happens on Base and Forming Day?

The exposed subgrade is compacted first, then wood or metal forms are staked along the driveway's finished edges to hold the concrete's shape and set its slope while it's still liquid. Base material, where the soil needs the extra support, goes down and gets compacted in lifts rather than dumped and rolled once, since a base that's compacted all at once often leaves soft pockets underneath that a single pass can't reach. Our concrete driveway page covers the thickness and strength spec this base work is built to meet; this guide is about the sequence, not the numbers behind it.

What Happens on Pour Day in Florida Heat?

Ready-mix concrete arrives by truck and is placed, screeded level and floated before the mix begins to set, a window that closes faster on a hot Florida afternoon than it does on a cool morning. Hot-weather guidance calls for starting early, before the sun and the slab temperature climb, keeping the subgrade damp without ponding water on it, and avoiding adding water to the mix once it's more than about an hour and a half old, since diluting curing concrete weakens the surface it was meant to strengthen (NRMCA CIP 12). Control joints are saw-cut within hours of finishing, timed to the concrete's set rather than to a fixed clock, so the cuts relieve shrinkage stress before an uncontrolled crack beats them to it (NRMCA CIP 6).

Why Does the Pour Get Scheduled Around the Weather, Not Just the Calendar?

A pour placed above about 95°F, or at an evaporation rate past roughly 0.2 lb per sq ft per hour, loses surface moisture faster than the slab underneath can keep up with, which shows up later as fine, closely spaced plastic-shrinkage cracking rather than a structural problem (ACI; ACI Concrete International, evaporation rate). An afternoon thunderstorm rolling in mid-pour is the other scheduling risk through Florida's wet season, roughly late May into mid-October, which is why crews here plan pours for early morning starts more often than not. Our rainy-season pour-scheduling guide and our guide to curing in Florida heat go deeper on both of those weather questions than fits in a step-by-step walkthrough.

How Long Does Curing Actually Take Before the Driveway Is Ready?

Curing and strength gain aren't the same clock. Industry guidance calls for at least 3 days of moist curing, by curing compound or wet curing, before the surface is considered set enough for light use, while the concrete itself keeps gaining strength for about 28 days before it reaches the mix design's full rated psi (NRMCA CIP 12). In practice that means a new driveway can usually take a car within about a week, but it's worth holding off on parking a loaded RV, a dumpster or heavy equipment on it until closer to that 28-day mark, since those loads ask more of the slab than ordinary daily traffic does.

Say You're Replacing a 24×24 ft Two-Car Driveway in Winter Garden

A 576 sq ft driveway in a Winter Garden subdivision follows the same sequence at a slightly larger scale: a day to demo and haul off the old slab, a day to compact the base and set forms for the two-car width, a pour day that typically wraps the placing and finishing in under half a day given the size, then the curing window before the owner's cars go back in the garage. A two-car driveway built in Florida market data at this size runs toward the lower end of the $6–$15 per sq ft installed range once the base work is straightforward and there's no old reinforced slab to cut through. Our concrete driveway cost guide breaks that pricing down further by size and finish.

Frequently asked questions

How many days does a concrete driveway installation take?

About a week from demolition through the point the slab can take light traffic, though a straightforward new pour with no old driveway to remove can move faster. Most of that week is excavation, base compaction and curing rather than the pour itself, which usually takes a few hours once the truck arrives.

What happens to the old driveway during a tear-out?

It's broken up and hauled off before any new work starts, and reinforced slabs with rebar or wire mesh take longer to demolish than plain concrete since the steel has to be cut free rather than just cracked loose. The exposed ground underneath is then excavated to the depth the new base and slab need together.

Why are control joints cut the same day as the pour?

The cuts are timed to the concrete's own set, not to a fixed schedule, so they relieve shrinkage stress in a controlled line before an uncontrolled crack forms somewhere else on the slab. Early-entry saws typically cut within a few hours of finishing; conventional saws follow a bit later the same day.

Does rain delay a concrete driveway pour in Florida?

An afternoon thunderstorm rolling in mid-pour is one of the main scheduling risks during the state's wet season, roughly late May into mid-October, which is why crews here plan early morning starts more than later ones. A pour that gets rained on before the surface sets can need patching or, in bad cases, part of the slab redone.

When does a new driveway reach full strength?

The surface is generally ready for light vehicle traffic after about a week once the minimum 3-day moist cure is complete, but the concrete keeps gaining strength for roughly 28 days before it reaches the mix design's full rated strength. Heavy loads like a loaded trailer or equipment are worth holding off until closer to that mark.
